notes: Solicitors Act time bar on detailed assessment of paid statute bills; statutory and inherent jurisdiction analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Time bar on detailed assessment of paid solicitor bills
key_facts: Radcliffes Le Brasseur rendered 13 bills to the Wickes defendants between January and November 2002; the first two were paid in full and the third mostly paid.
The firm issued proceedings in July 2003 for £61,392.99 plus interest on unpaid bills.
The defendants counterclaimed for detailed assessment of paid and unpaid bills under the Solicitors Act 1974.
Master Leslie ordered detailed assessment of unpaid bills and an enquiry as to whether paid bills numbered 251450 and 252025 could be assessed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Enquiry following a case management order on whether fully paid statute bills could be subject to detailed assessment more than 12 months after payment.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants held not entitled to detailed assessment of the two fully paid bills; section 70(4) time bar applied and inherent jurisdiction could not be invoked.
enrichment.ratio: Where invoices were clearly intended and treated as statute bills rather than payments on account, section 70(4) of the Solicitors Act 1974 bars detailed assessment more than 12 months after payment; the court's inherent jurisdiction to refer bills for taxation does not create a free-standing cause of action and cannot override that statutory bar in these circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether paid bills were statute bills or part of an entire retainer
Whether section 70(4) barred assessment of bills paid over a year before proceedings
Whether inherent jurisdiction under Re Park could order taxation outside the statutory time limit
Whether the bills satisfied section 69(2) narrative requirements
linked_authorities: Harrison v Tew [1990] 2 AC 523
Re Park [1889] 41 ChD 326
Ralph Hume Garry v Gwillim [2003] 1 CostLR 77
Abedi v Penningtons [2000] 2 Costs LR 205
Turner v Polomo [1999] 4 All ER 353
Allen v Jarvis [1869] LR 4 Ch App 616

confidence.notes: Statutory time bar finding and rejection of inherent jurisdiction are explicit. Retainer letter evidence was not proved.

notes: Libyan deportation Article 3 appeal; fresh evidence refusal and risk assessment upholding are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Libyan deportation and Article 3 risk appeal

statutes_considered.title: Convention relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: The appellant, a Libyan national resident in the UK since 1979, was convicted of indecent assault and rape and faced deportation to Libya.
An adjudicator found no real risk of Article 2 or Article 3 breach on return, relying partly on FCO assurances obtained at senior Libyan official level.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissed the appeal after detailed review of country evidence.
On appeal the appellant sought to adduce fresh evidence from Dr George Joffé about monitoring of Libyan students and press reporting.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against the IAT's dismissal of a human rights challenge to deportation to Libya.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; fresh evidence refused and the IAT's Article 3 assessment held not perverse.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence on asylum and Article 3 appeals from the IAT is governed by Ladd v Marshall and should not be admitted where it could have been obtained for the tribunal hearing; the IAT was entitled to rely on high-level diplomatic assurances and to find no real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment on return.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT's Article 3 risk assessment was perverse or involved an error of law
Whether fresh evidence from Dr Joffé should be admitted on appeal
Whether Libyan authorities would know of past asylum status or press reports
Whether delay in enforcing deportation would create suspicion on return
linked_authorities: E and R v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 49
Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489
Al-Mehdawi v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1990] 1 AC 876
Arif [1999] Imm AR 271

confidence.notes: Appeal dismissal, fresh evidence refusal and Ladd v Marshall application are explicit. Country risk findings are evaluative.

notes: Recruitment commission contract construction on wrongful dismissal; appeal outcome and ET jurisdiction cap clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Recruitment commission payable after wrongful dismissal

statutes_considered.title: Employment Tribunals Extension of Jurisdiction (England and Wales) Order 1994

key_facts: Nicholas Brand was a contract sales consultant for Compro Computer Services Ltd under a commission compensation plan.
Compro summarily dismissed him on 26 July 2001 when the Watford contract division closed, denying commission payable in arrears for June and July sales.
The employment tribunal found the dismissal fair for redundancy but awarded damages for one month's commission after finding wrongful termination of notice.
Clause 6(1) of the plan required the employee to remain in full-time employment at all times to qualify for commission payments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on construction of commission entitlement after summary dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; ET and EAT erred in construing clause 6(1) as denying commission earned before dismissal; total breach of contract award capped at £25,000.
enrichment.ratio: Commission earned when signed contractor timesheets are received is payable notwithstanding payment in arrears after dismissal; clause 6(1) merely assumes continued full-time status and does not deprive an employee of commission on sales achieved before wrongful termination.
legal_issues: Whether clause 6(1) required employment at the payroll payment date
When commission was earned under clause 4.1 of the compensation plan
Construction of employment contract and commission memorandum together
Effect of the £25,000 ET jurisdiction limit on breach of contract claims
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

confidence.notes: Contract construction reasoning and substituted £25,000 award are clearly articulated by the Court of Appeal.

notes: Bareboat charter loss payment discount date; preliminary issue and appeal dismissal are clear despite drafting defects.

enrichment.short_title: Bareboat charter loss payment discount date
key_facts: The semi-submersible platform Spirit of Columbus sank after an explosion in March 2001 under complex bareboat charter and sub-charter arrangements.
Petromec and related parties disputed whether future hire under the loss payment clause should be discounted to the date of total loss or 90 days later.
The difference in LIBOR movement was about US$2.5 million on a payment exceeding US$330 million.
Tomlinson J declared the correct loss payment at US$334,557,499.34 on a preliminary issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Commercial Court preliminary issue on construction of the loss payment discount date under bareboat charter agreements.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; discounting to be to the date payment is declared due at the end of the 90-day period, not the date of total loss.
enrichment.ratio: Under clause 11 of the bareboat charter, the loss payment crystallises at the end of the 90-day period following total loss rather than on day one; discounting future fixed hire to the date of loss would produce absurd results including overdue interest on unpaid instalments not yet due.
legal_issues: Whether loss payment discounting runs from the date of total loss or 90 days later
Distinction between clause 11 total loss and clause 13 termination regimes
Whether a declaration of loss payment was required before sums became due
Effect of sloppy drafting on construction of liquidated damages provisions

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue outcome and clause 11/13 distinction are clearly reasoned. Underlying total loss facts are background.

notes: Long-running boundary dispute with overlapping Taylor v Lawrence, allocation and Grepe v Loam applications; procedural holdings are clear but history is dense.

enrichment.short_title: Bonvilston boundary dispute procedural appeals refused
key_facts: A boundary dispute between Mr Parker at the Great Barn and Mr Hutchings at Lillypot Farm in Bonvilston began with a district judge's arbitration award in 1997.
Judge Jones found for Mr Parker after a four-day site visit in 2000; Jacob J refused permission to appeal on proportionality grounds.
Neuberger J refused allocation to the multi-track under the slip rule and later refused a Taylor v Lawrence application to reopen the refusal of permission to appeal.
Mr Hutchings sought further permission to appeal and to challenge a Grepe v Loam order requiring prior permission for further applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal on allocation, Taylor v Lawrence reopening, and a Grepe v Loam order in long-running boundary litigation.
enrichment.outcome: All three applications dismissed; no jurisdiction to appeal further after Taylor v Lawrence refusal; Grepe v Loam order upheld.
enrichment.ratio: There is no further right of appeal after a judge refuses to reopen a permission decision under Taylor v Lawrence; a second appeal requires an important point of principle or compelling reason, which credibility and allocation complaints in a small boundary dispute do not provide.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Jones could allocate the case to the multi-track under the slip rule
Whether Neuberger J's Taylor v Lawrence refusal could be appealed
Whether a Grepe v Loam order could be challenged out of time
Whether alleged witness lies justify a second appeal
linked_authorities: Taylor v Lawrence [2002] EWCA Civ 90
Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 2) [2003] EWCA Civ 1113

confidence.notes: Procedural refusals are explicit but the litigation spans many years and overlapping applications.

notes: DDA s.5(4) justification defence analysis is detailed but ratio and remittal order are clear.

enrichment.short_title: DDA justification of failure to make reasonable adjustments
key_facts: Mr Collins, a carpenter's labourer at the National Theatre, lost part of a finger in a bench saw accident and developed painful neuromas.
He refused recommended surgery and the theatre terminated his employment after capability assessments raised safety concerns.
The employment tribunal found a section 6 duty to make adjustments had been breached but the EAT allowed the employer's appeal relying on Jones v Post Office.
The appeal asked whether an unreasonable failure to make adjustments could nevertheless be justified under section 5(4).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on construction of the justification defence to failure to make reasonable adjustments under the Disability Discrimination Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; employment tribunal decision restored and claim remitted on remedy; section 5(4) cannot justify factors already rejected as unreasonable under section 6.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5(4) of the DDA must be construed differently from section 5(3); an employer cannot justify a breach of the section 6 reasonable adjustment duty by re-litigating grounds already evaluated as unreasonable, though section 5(4) may still apply to factors outside the section 6 inquiry.
legal_issues: Whether section 5(4) permits justification of an objectively unreasonable failure to adjust
Relationship between sections 5(3), 5(4) and 6 of the DDA
Effect of Jones v Post Office on adjustment failures
Whether the National Theatre's dismissal was separately unfair
linked_authorities: Jones v Post Office [2001] EWCA Civ 558
H J Heinz & Co Ltd v Kenrick [2000] IRLR 144

confidence.notes: Statutory construction holding and remittal order are explicit. Unfair dismissal was not argued on appeal.

notes: Civil court jurisdiction over cattle removal after cruelty disqualification; appeal dismissal and negative injunction scope are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Council cannot remove disqualified owners' cattle by injunction
key_facts: Lionel Tongue and his sons were convicted of cattle cruelty and disqualified for life from custody of farm animals.
They continued to keep cattle on several Worcestershire farms in breach of the disqualification orders.
Worcestershire County Council sought a Chancery injunction authorising entry onto the Tongues' land to remove all livestock and dispose of them.
Neuberger J held the civil court had no jurisdiction to make the positive removal order sought, though a prohibitory injunction was available.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of mandatory injunctive relief to remove cattle from land of persons disqualified under animal cruelty legislation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; civil court has no jurisdiction to authorise removal and disposal of defendants' cattle beyond restraining breach of disqualification orders.
enrichment.ratio: While a local authority may invoke civil proceedings under section 222 to restrain breach of the criminal law, it cannot obtain mandatory orders to remove and dispose of animals belonging to disqualified owners where Parliament has prescribed criminal remedies and has not conferred equivalent civil powers on the county court.
legal_issues: Whether section 222 Local Government Act 1972 confers jurisdiction for mandatory cattle removal
Whether the Council had sufficient interest under section 37 Supreme Court Act 1981
Distinction between enforcing criminal law and filling gaps in it
Whether orders under the 2000 Act limited relief to animals the subject of cruelty proceedings

Stoke-on-Trent City Council v B and Q plc [1984] AC 754
Chief Constable of Leicestershire v M [1989] 1 WLR 20
Chief Constable of Kent v V [1983] QB 34

notes: Carousel fraud illegality defence rejected; proximity analysis and judgment sum are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Carousel fraud seller may recover CPU sale price
key_facts: 21st Century Logistic Solutions Ltd, a missing-trader phoenix company, sold 7,220 Intel CPUs to Madysen Ltd for £905,220 including VAT.
Darren King, the directing mind of 21stC, intended to defraud HMCE of output VAT; Madysen was unaware of that intention.
Madysen paid £913,680 from Pycom and reported suspicious payment instructions to HMCE; funds were frozen and 21stC went into liquidation.
Madysen pleaded illegality to resist paying the agreed price for goods delivered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a liquidator's claim for the price of goods sold and delivered where the buyer pleaded ex turpi causa illegality.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant for £905,220; fraudulent VAT intention at contract formation was too remote to render the sale contract unenforceable.
enrichment.ratio: A contract for sale of goods entered into with a dishonest intention to evade VAT is not necessarily unenforceable where the fraud would only be completed by a later failure to account to HMCE; the lawful contract itself merely provided opportunity for the fraud and the buyer's ignorance prevents mutual illegality.
legal_issues: Whether 21stC's missing-trader intention rendered the sale contract illegal
Proximity between fraudulent intent and the contract under ex turpi causa principles
Distinction from Alexander v Rayson and Napier v National Business Agency
Whether liquidation and HMCE's creditor status affected enforceability

Napier v National Business Agency Ltd [1951] 2 All ER 264

notes: Section 459 petition with fiduciary breach finding, ransom-strip valuation debate and strong judicial criticism of Lord Ashcroft's tactics.

enrichment.short_title: Section 459 petition over ISS takeover asset sale
key_facts: ISS acquired over 96% of RCO (Holdings) Ltd but Lord Ashcroft's Rock (Nominees) Ltd retained a blocking minority stake.
In November 2000 the company sold its operating subsidiaries to ISS UK for £30,117,784, equivalent to 280p per share.
Rock petitioned under section 459 alleging undervalue and breach of fiduciary duty by conflicted ISS directors.
Peter Smith J found fiduciary breaches but held the sale price fair and dismissed the petition as a greenmail tactic.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against dismissal of an unfair prejudice petition concerning an intra-group asset sale to squeeze out a minority shareholder.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; sale not at undervalue and no unfair prejudice; cross-appeal allowed setting aside fiduciary breach finding as no harm was done.
enrichment.ratio: Where ISS would not pay more than 280p and could place the company in liquidation to sell assets on the open market with no alternative bidder, the sale price was the best reasonably obtainable and Rock suffered no unfair prejudice despite defective sale mechanics.
legal_issues: Whether the sale of Group shares was at an undervalue
Whether ISS synergies justified a higher ransom price
Whether conflicted directors breached fiduciary duties
Admissibility of the February Report as valuation evidence
linked_authorities: Re Ring Tower (No 2) [1989] BCLC 427

confidence.notes: Undervalue conclusion and appeal dismissal are clear. Fiduciary breach finding was reversed on cross-appeal; judge's commentary on tactics is extensive.

notes: Business rates valuation of highway microcell mast site; Poplar principles application and agreed figures are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Rates for mobile phone mast on highway land

statutes_considered.title: Valuation for Rating (Plant and Machinery) Regulations 1994
New Roads and Street Works Act 1991

key_facts: Orange PCS operated a microcell mast on a grass verge of a public highway in Carlton-in-Lindrick, Nottinghamshire.
Under the Telecommunications Code operators may install apparatus on highways without payment to the highway authority or adjacent landowners.
The site was rated at £2,200 from 1 November 1999; Orange contended the land value should be nil because of free Code occupation.
It was agreed that if Orange succeeded the rateable value would be £100 (mast only); if not, £1,100 including £1,000 for land occupation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on correct rating valuation approach for a telecommunications hereditament on highway land.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; free occupation under the Code does not reduce rateable value; agreed rateable value of £1,100 upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Under Poplar Assessment Committee v Roberts, the statutory rating hypothesis values beneficial occupation of the hereditament and not the actual rent payable; a telecommunications operator's personal right to free highway occupation under the Code is not determinative of that value.
legal_issues: Whether free Telecommunications Code occupation requires a nil land value for rating
Application of Poplar v Roberts to statutory rather than contractual rent restrictions
Relevance of comparable rents on private land for microcell sites
Principle of reality in rating valuation
